summary: The narrator wakes on Checker's couch after a drugged sleep, still groggy and aching, and is told by Arthur that Martinez has a brain tumor that has probably been growing for a while and that she has only days or weeks left and is unlikely to wake again. The narrator is shocked and feels guilt over having not worried about Martinez, and is torn between a conscience and a wish to escape the loss of the proof that could save him. Earlier, he privately resolved to pursue that proof carefully and wait to see the Feds' plan, and Checker has said D.J. may not have been caught.
one_line: Groggy after painkillers, the narrator learns from Arthur that Martinez has a terminal brain tumor and is consumed by guilt and despair.
key_facts: The narrator sleeps on Checker's couch under narcotic painkillers and, for once, does not dream.
The narrator tells Checker that the pyro dude, D.J., was probably not at the location and that they may not have gotten him.
Checker responds 'Okay. Thanks.' and says he may want to talk about it another time.
When the narrator wakes, Checker and Pilar are gone and Arthur is working on a laptop across the room.
The narrator waves off the painkillers offered by Arthur, saying he wants to be awake.
Arthur tells the narrator that Martinez has a brain tumor.
Arthur says the docs estimate Martinez has only days, maybe weeks, left and is unlikely to wake up again.
The narrator whispers 'No' in response to the news about Martinez.
The narrator admits he had not been worried about Martinez, even after everything that happened.
The narrator feels guilt and wishes he were a better person or had no conscience at all.
The narrator considers drinking himself into a stupor as a way to escape his despair.
The narrator had promised himself he would obtain proof without going too far this time and would wait to see what the Feds' play was.
The narrator names Martinez, the NSA and the DHS as parties whose positions he must consider regarding the proof he needs.
